title: What an Organism Has to Do

scenes.visual: Title: What an Organism Has to Do. Show a barley plant, honeybee and human beside five empty checklist spaces.

scenes.tts: Every multicellular organism faces the same five problems. Get energy and materials. Exchange and move them, including wastes. Keep its inside relatively stable. Resist damage and invasion. And leave descendants. This checklist connects a barley plant, a honeybee and a human. Every solution carries a cost. To understand a body, we need to ask how it solves these problems, and how its solutions evolved.

scenes.visual: Reveal the five course checklist items in spoken order: energy and materials; exchange and transport, including wastes; internal stability; defense; continuation of a lineage. Connect all five to the plant, bee and human. Keep the checklist visible as the course map; label it a teaching checklist.

scenes.tts: Plants capture light and absorb water and minerals through their roots. Materials must reach every cell, and wastes must leave. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment relatively stable. Defense resists damage and invasion. Reproduction continues a lineage. A honeybee worker can help pass on copies of its genes by raising close relatives.

scenes.visual: Expand each checklist item with a lesson example: light at leaves and water/minerals at roots; transport to cells and wastes leaving; internal stability; defense; worker bee helping raise relatives. Show reproduction at lineage level, rather than implying that every individual reproduces.

scenes.tts: A barley leaf shows the cost of exchange. Carbon dioxide enters through tiny pores called stomata. Water vapour leaves through those same pores. When the stomata are open, both things happen at once.

scenes.visual: Highlight exchange on the checklist. Show a barley leaf cross-section: waxy outer layer, guard cells around a stoma, and wet internal cell walls. Carbon dioxide enters through the pore; water evaporates from internal walls and diffuses out.

scenes.tts: Your lungs face a similar bargain. Gas must dissolve in a wet film before entering cells. A wet surface in air loses water. In ordinary, drier air, each breath carries water away. Neither solution escapes the cost.

scenes.visual: Compare the leaf with a lung sheltered inside the chest. Locate the moist exchange surface at the air-sac lining. Show airways moistening incoming air and recovering some water on exhalation, with water still leaving in the breath.

scenes.tts: Water-use efficiency is carbon gained divided by water lost. Here are made-up leaves, not barley data. Leaf A gains twenty micromoles of carbon dioxide and loses five millimoles of water, per square metre per second. Its efficiency is four point zero.
scenes.narration: Water-use efficiency is carbon gained divided by water lost. Here are made-up leaves, not barley data. Leaf A gains 20 µmol of CO2 and loses 5 mmol of water, per m² per s. Its efficiency is 4.0.
scenes.caption: Water-use efficiency is carbon gained divided by water lost. Here are made-up leaves, not barley data. Leaf A gains 20 µmol of CO2 and loses 5 mmol of water, per m² per s. Its efficiency is 4.0.
scenes.visual: Show carbon gained / water lost. Label illustrative values, not barley data. Leaf A: assimilation 20 µmol CO2 per m² per s; transpiration 5 mmol H2O per m² per s; efficiency 4.0 µmol CO2 per mmol H2O.

scenes.tts: Leaf B gains sixteen and loses three. Its efficiency is five point three. When water is scarce, B keeps more water per unit of carbon. When water is plentiful and carbon limits growth, A gains more.
scenes.narration: Leaf B gains 16 and loses 3. Its efficiency is 5.3. When water is scarce, B keeps more water per unit of carbon. When water is plentiful and carbon limits growth, A gains more.
scenes.caption: Leaf B gains 16 and loses 3. Its efficiency is 5.3. When water is scarce, B keeps more water per unit of carbon. When water is plentiful and carbon limits growth, A gains more.
scenes.visual: Keep identical units on both leaves. Add B: 16 µmol CO2 per m² per s, 3 mmol H2O per m² per s, efficiency 5.3 µmol CO2 per mmol H2O. Show water scarcity favouring B and plentiful water with carbon-limited growth favouring A.

scenes.tts: Why do structures fit what they do? Natural selection acts on inherited variation. Over generations, traits linked to greater reproductive success can become more common. But the fit is never perfect. Trade-offs link gains to costs. Selection works with inherited structures. Some changes spread by chance, and some features are by-products. Evolution has no preconceived ideal.

scenes.visual: Move from the exchange example to inherited variation across generations and differential reproductive success. Then show three constraints: carbon gain versus water loss; shared ancestral limb bones reshaped in human arm, bat wing and whale flipper; chance and by-products. Avoid a ladder of progress or an ideal endpoint.

scenes.tts: We also need complementary questions. Mechanism asks how guard cells open and close a pore. Development asks how genes set the number of stomata. Adaptive significance asks how density affects survival and reproduction. History asks how density changed across a lineage. The first pair concerns an organism’s lifetime. The second concerns evolution. A full account needs both.

scenes.visual: Show four questions grouped in two pairs. Proximate: mechanism, guard-cell movement; development, genes and stomatal number. Ultimate: adaptive significance, survival and reproduction in an environment; history, changes across a lineage. Finish with all five organismal problems framing these complementary questions.
Return to the five-item course checklist beside the plant, bee and human. End card: What an Organism Has to Do.
